title: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark

model.params_source: assumed (paper silent on decoding; the public evaluation script in TIGER-AI-Lab/MMLU-Pro uses temperature 0, top_p 1, max_tokens 4000)

task.approximation: none (same 12,032 test items, same 5 validation exemplars per category; option lines rendered one per line as in the public eval script because Table 7's rendering collapses line breaks)

items.config_or_split: default / test (exemplars: default / validation, 70 rows = 5 per category)

fields_paper.options: options (list of up to 10 strings, lettered A-J in order)
fields_paper.label: gold {answer: letter, n_options: k} (hook; k feeds the paper's random fallback)

placeholders.question: items.question
placeholders.few_shot_block:
hook: the 5 validation-split exemplars of the item's category, each 'Question: ..
Options: A. ..
Answer: Let's think step by step. .. The answer is (X).

' (cot_content with its 'A: ' prefix removed)

prompt.few_shot: k=5 fixed exemplars per category from the MMLU-Pro validation split (Sec. 4 / Appendix A.2)
prompt.source_location: Table 7 (5-shot CoT prompt example in physics) and Appendix A.2
prompt.verbatim: full (instruction line, exemplar layout and the trailing 'Answer: Let's think step by step.' copied from Table 7; the line breaks between options are restored per the public eval script)

placeholders_paper.category: items.category (e.g. physics), lowercase as in Table 7
placeholders_paper.question: items.question
placeholders_paper.options: items.options formatted as 'A. ...\nB. ...' (one option per line, letters A-J)

output.parse: hook: regex answer is \(?([A-J])\)? ; fallback [aA]nswer:\s*([A-J]) ; else seeded random option (paper fallback, count logged)
output.postprocess: take the first match of the primary regex, else the fallback; if both fail select a seeded random option (paper's fallback) and log the count
output.parse_paper: regex answer is \(?([A-J])\)? ; fallback regex [aA]nswer:\s*([A-J]) (Sec. 4 Answer Extraction)

metric.name: accuracy
metric.definition: share of test items whose extracted letter equals the answer field, in percent
metric.original_location: Table 2, row GPT-4-Turbo, column Overall (5-shot CoT)

notes: Roughly 2.5K input tokens (5 CoT exemplars) and 300 output tokens per call at gpt-4-turbo prices (~$0.035/call). The repository's instruction line differs slightly ('...then output the answer in the format of "The answer is (X)" at the end.'); the paper's Table 7 wording is used. Per-subject subsets (e.g. physics 1,299 items, Table 2 column) are cheaper partial checks. GPT-4-Turbo also served in dataset construction (answer extraction, option augmentation). || [normalize 2026-09-07] hf parquet default/test (12,032 rows) and default/validation (70 rows; question_id, question, options, answer, answer_index, cot_content, category, src) verified; options_lettered(options) yields the 'A. ..' lines. || [hooks_2 2026-09-07] few-shot assembly from the validation split and the random fallback live in the hook; prepare verified (12,032 items; the default --cap 40 subsets the run, raise the cap for the full set). || [triage 2026-09-09] DEVIATION, pipeline verified: the cost-cap subset is a seeded random draw over the whole test set (ids 85..12244; per-category shares within 1.7 points of the full set; reweighting the per-category accuracies to the full shares gives 67.4 vs 68.0). Extraction: 1,627 primary regex, 0 secondary, 25 random fallback (paper's rule; 13 of the 25 would be caught by the repository script's third-stage 'last standalone letter' regex, which the paper does not describe), 0 truncated at max_tokens 4000, no 'answer is **X**' cases. Per category vs Table 2 (same snapshot gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09): math 75.4 vs 62.8, physics 72.7 vs 61.0, engineering 50.8 vs 35.9, law 45.2 vs 51.2, history 64.8 vs 67.7, psychology 77.7 vs 78.3 - the gap sits entirely in the quantitative subjects. The dataset's post-publication answer-key corrections (changelog 2024-07/08/09, a handful of math/engineering IDs) are too few to explain it; the pattern is consistent with the paper's run losing long CoT answers (truncation or extraction failure -> random option) on math/physics/engineering. Full-set re-run would cost about $420.
